Small sandeel Ammodytes tobianus attains a maximum recorded standard length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], a modest size that reflects its position as a key forage fish in coastal North Atlantic ecosystems. Individuals typically reach the onset of reproductive maturity upon achieving a standard length of around 13 centimeters [Lp = around 13 centimeters], a size threshold that ensures sufficient body volume for gonad development and successful spawning. At the time of first reproduction, the average wet weight of a mature individual is approximately 6 grams [Wwp = approximately 6 grams], a mass that aligns well with the length-weight relationship derived for this species. The greatest body mass recorded for adult sandeels, representing the asymptotic wet weight, is 22.6 grams [Wwi = 22.6 grams], a value that is consistent with the typical slender, elongate body plan of ammodytids. This ultimate mass is reached only after several years of growth in productive feeding grounds.

During the spawning season, female Ammodytes tobianus produce large numbers of small pelagic eggs, a strategy common among batch-spawning teleosts. Based on fecundity estimates derived from the closely related congener Ammodytes marinus, the maximum daily egg production rate for a female small sandeel is achieved when water temperatures remain near 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C], with an average output of approximately 25,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 25,000 eggs per spawning event] and one spawning event per year [F_R_i = one spawning event per year]. This high reproductive output is partially offset by the extremely small size of the newly hatched larvae. The wet weight at birth, estimated from an egg diameter of 0.9 millimeters, is a mere 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to support the pelagic larval stage before the onset of exogenous feeding. These minute prolarvae drift in the plankton for several weeks, facing substantial mortality pressure before they develop the ability to capture prey.

The embryonic development of small sandeel is strongly temperature-dependent, with a clear relationship between thermal regime and the duration of the egg stage. At a stable incubation temperature of 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C], the age at birth, defined as the period from fertilisation to eclosion of the yolk-sac larva, is approximately 19 days [ab = approximately 19 days]. This hatching period is relatively brief compared to that of many other temperate marine teleosts, likely an adaptation that reduces the vulnerability of demersal eggs to benthic predators. Upon emergence, the prolarvae measure only a few millimeters in length and rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves until the mouth opens and the yolk-sac is fully resorbed. The transition to exogenous feeding marks a critical bottleneck in the life cycle, as larvae must encounter suitably sized copepod nauplii within a narrow window of time or face starvation.

Longevity in Ammodytes tobianus is constrained by its rapid life-history pace and high natural mortality rates in the pelagic environment. The maximum lifespan documented for this species under natural thermal conditions, at approximately 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C], is 2,555 days [am = 2,555 days], which corresponds to roughly seven years [am = roughly seven years]. This lifespan is intermediate among forage fish, being shorter than that of some larger clupeids but longer than that of many small gobies. The oldest individuals are typically found in cooler, higher-latitude populations where metabolic rates are depressed and growth is slower. Senescence in sandeels is associated with a decline in body condition and a reduction in spawning frequency during the final year of life, after which natural mortality removes most surviving adults before the onset of the eighth winter.

Habitat selection in small sandeel is strongly linked to sediment type, as this species requires well-oxygenated sandy substrates into which it can burrow for refuge from predators and during overwintering periods. Juveniles and adults alike exhibit this burrowing behaviour, which is facilitated by the pointed snout and streamlined body plan that allows rapid penetration into the substrate, with adults reaching a maximum standard length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters]. The species forms large, dense schools in the water column during active foraging periods, primarily targeting copepods and other small zooplankton. The burrowing habit imposes a seasonal constraint on the energy budget, as individuals must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves during the summer growing season to sustain themselves through winter quiescence. This ecological strategy, combined with high fecundity and a relatively short generation time, positions Ammodytes tobianus as a critical trophic link between planktonic production and higher-level predators such as gadoids, seabirds, and marine mammals throughout its North Atlantic range.
